title: Prompts Are Code

post.author: u/night_press_yannick
post.title: I'm the night printer at a print shop. At 06:00 I had 412 wedding invitations for three weddings, and every one begins "Dear Hortense". There is no Hortense on any guest list.

blocks.text: I'm Yannick, the night printer at Larkwhistle Press, a print shop. Couples order wedding invitations from us, one card per guest, each with a few warm lines written for that guest. A language model, a program that reads text and writes text back, drafts those lines. Overnight our printer prints them, two cards a minute.

The model is sent written instructions with every card, called the prompt. Ours says what to write, gives an example letter to copy the style of, and ends with the guest's details. It lives in a text box on our admin page, the shop's private web page for running things. Sibylla, our day manager, writes it.

The prompt has slots: gaps marked with curly brackets, like {guest_name}. Before each card, a small program called the template filler takes five values from the order sheet: the couple, the date, the venue, the guest's name and the reply-by date. It drops each value into its slot, like filling in the blanks on a form. A value with no slot is quietly left out. Nothing warns anyone.

Sibylla wrote the prompt in March and has changed it six times since, always by day. She marks each change on the wall calendar, so I can number them: versions 1 to 7. The box itself keeps no versions, no saved and numbered copy of each earlier text. Saving replaces it.
Every afternoon at 16:00 she prints a proof card, one test card from the night's first order, and reads it. Each of those seven versions passed its proof card.

Yesterday's 16:00 proof was right, on version 7, saved on 8 October. At 22:40 the February couple emailed asking for a warmer tone. At 23:10, at home, Sibylla rewrote the example letter on her phone. At 01:00 the run started by itself: 412 cards for three weddings, of 176, 139 and 97 guests. It finished at 04:26.

At 06:00 I squared the stacks for the van. The cards come out face down; I count them, I don't read them. One slid face up. Each line below shows the card number, the guest on the order sheet, and the card's first words.

001  Chidera   Dear Hortense, we would love you
002  Paavo     Dear Hortense, we would love you
003  Thandiwe  Dear Hortense, we would love you
All 412 begin Dear Hortense. There is no Hortense on any of the three guest lists.

Hortense is the name in the example letter. At 07:00 Sibylla came in and we read the box together. Her new letter is there, but the line under it is gone: This card is for: {guest_name}. Selecting the old letter on a small screen, she took one line too many.

Bottom row: the printer, idle until 01:00, printing from 01:00 to 04:26, then idle. blocks.text: Mr Tibbald, the owner, has card stock for a reprint, and the couples need theirs in the post by Monday. What should we change before the next edit?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nobody called Hortense is writing to your guests. A language model (a1e03) sees only what it is sent for each card, and it fills a gap with the likeliest words. Given an example letter and no name, the likeliest name is the one in front of it. Two questions. Which values did the template filler hand over at 01:00, and which slots did the prompt still have? And what does the box hold of version 7 now?

replies.author: u/night_press_yannick
replies.text: It filled all five, as always. The prompt now has four slots: couple, date, venue and reply-by date. So guest_name was filled and thrown away 412 times. And the box holds only last night's text. Version 7 survives as the 8 October proof card on the wall: a printed card, not the prompt.

replies.author: u/gradient_ghost
replies.text: One phrase you may want. Comparing a prompt's slots with the values the code fills, one by one, is called checking it against the code. Here the code is your template filler. Whether that helps is your call.

comments.author: u/just_words_haruki
comments.text: Prompts are just text. Keeping numbered versions is for engineers' code, not an invitation template. What went wrong is a tired person on a phone at 23:10. Lock the page: only the owner edits it, only at the shop's computer, on a proper screen. One careful person, one place, nothing to install.

replies.author: u/night_press_yannick
replies.text: Mr Tibbald says he'd happily do it. He answers couples' emails at the shop in the evenings, after closing.

comments.author: u/february_bride_bogdana
comments.text: We're the 97. I asked for warmer, and I'm sorry it went like this. Couples don't care how a shop stores its words. Have a person read every card in the morning before any go in the post. That's what a print shop is for.

replies.author: u/night_press_yannick
replies.text: Sibylla timed herself on this morning's stack: about 20 seconds a card.

reply.prompt: Mr Tibbald wants a rule in place before the next prompt change. What should Larkwhistle change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Lock the prompt page so only the owner can edit it, and only from the shop's own computer.
options.part2: Mr Tibbald locked the admin page to his own login on the shop's computer. We replayed last night in the sim, with the February couple's email reaching him at 23:10 and the same slip on a bigger screen: one line too many selected. At 01:00 the run printed 412 cards by 04:26, every one beginning "Dear Hortense, we would love you to join us." The lock changed who typed, not what reached the printer. The new text still went straight to the night's run, with no check and nothing to go back to.
options.senior: Limiting who can change a prompt is reasonable, and it is not change control. Careful people make slips too, and the dangerous part was that any save went straight to the next run, unchecked, with the old text gone. Keep the access rule if you like, but also make every change a numbered version, run checks on it before it can go live, and keep the last good version one step away.

options.text: Keep prompts as numbered versions, checked against the code, proofed on 5 cards first.
options.part2: We moved the prompt out of the box into numbered files, kept in the same history as the template filler's code. Every save now runs three things. A slot check compares the prompt's slots with the five values the code fills. A ten-card eval, a test run on ten made-up guests, needs each card to begin with that guest's name and carry the reply-by date. And a proof batch: a new version prints only the run's first 5 cards, behind a flag, a switch that keeps the rest on the old version until someone approves. We replayed last night. Sibylla's 23:10 edit saved as version 8, and the slot check failed it at once: the code fills guest_name; version 8 has no slot for it. Version 7 stayed live, and 412 right cards were done by 04:26. With only the proof batch on, the run stopped at 5 cards, at 01:02:30; one click rolled back to version 7, and 412 right cards were done by 04:28:30.
options.senior: Treat a prompt like code, because it changes what the product does just as code does. Keep it as a numbered version in the same history as the code that fills it, so every change has a number, a date and an author, and the last good one is one switch away. Check each version against the code: every value the code fills needs a slot, and every slot needs a value. Run a small eval on every save. Then roll the new version out to a few outputs behind a flag before the rest, the way Dead Letter s6e08, Canary in the Mine, rolls out code.

options.text: Have a person proofread all 412 invitations in the morning before any go in the post.
options.verdict: Too late: the paper is printed
options.part2: Sibylla read every card from 07:00, at about 20 seconds each. She finished at 09:17:20 and found all 412 wrong. Nothing went in the post, which is something. But the cards were already printed: 412 wasted, and the reprint waited for the next night's run. And nothing would stop the next late edit from doing it again.
options.senior: A check after the work is done finds the damage; it doesn't prevent it. Reading 412 cards takes over two hours and still costs every card. Put the check before the expensive step: test a new version on a few cards, and stop the run if they're wrong. Keep a person's eye where it is cheap, on 5 proof cards, not on 412 finished ones.

options.text: Retype last week's prompt from memory tonight and run the whole print again from scratch.
options.part2: At 07:30 Sibylla retyped last week's prompt from memory, and that night's 01:00 run printed 412 again by 04:26. Every card had the right name. None had the reply-by date: her retyped text had no {rsvp_by} slot, and the template filler dropped the date 412 times without a word. A second 412 cards, and all of them wrong in a new way.
options.senior: Retyping is the honest fix for tonight when nothing was kept, and it shows the real gap: there was no version to return to, so the old prompt had to be rebuilt from memory, and memory dropped a line. Keep every version, so going back is one switch, not a rewrite. And check every version against the code, which would have caught this missing slot at once.

sim.title: Replay the night at Larkwhistle Press
sim.lede: You're Yannick at 22:00, before the couple's email, with version 7 live and nothing printed. No real model runs here: a card begins with the guest's name only if the prompt has a {guest_name} slot; with no slot it copies the example letter's "Dear Hortense", and with no {rsvp_by} slot it has no reply-by date. The code always fills five values: couple, date, venue, guest_name, rsvp_by. Three weddings: 176, 139 and 97 guests, 412 cards, printed two a minute from 01:00. You choose which prompt is saved at 23:10: one of versions 1 to 8, or a retyped copy. Then switch on any of: prompts kept as numbered versions, a slot check that compares slots with those five values, a ten-card eval (ten made-up test guests, each card must begin with its own name and carry the date), a proof batch (a new version prints only the first 5 cards, then waits for a person), a lock on the admin page, and a person reading every card from 07:00, 20 seconds each.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Run the night. 412 cards, every one "Dear Hortense", done at 04:26:00. Set the prompt to versions 1 to 7 and run each: 412 right names every time. Back on version 8, switch on the slot check alone: the run stops before printing, and with no versions kept there is nothing to print from. Keep numbered versions too, and version 7 prints 412 right cards. Then try the proof batch alone and press Roll back to version 7, the button that switches back to the last good version.

explain.oneLine: No guest called Hortense; the name was in the example letter. At 23:10 an edit on a phone removed the line holding the {guest_name} slot. The template filler quietly dropped the name it had no slot for, the model copied the only name it was given, and with no versions, no checks and no proof after 16:00, the 01:00 run printed all 412.

steps.title: How one card is made.
steps.text: Each card runs in steps. First the template filler reads the order sheet and takes five values: couple, date, venue, guest_name and rsvp_by, the reply-by date. Second it puts each value into the prompt's slot of the same name. Third the prompt goes to the model, which writes the card's lines, copying the example letter's style. Last the printer prints it, two cards a minute. From version 1 in March to version 7 on 8 October, every version had all five slots, so every card began with its own guest's name. What can go wrong: the prompt and the filler are written separately, and nothing checks that they still fit.

steps.title: Why the name vanished without an error.
steps.text: At 23:10 Sibylla's new example letter replaced the old one, and her selection took the next line too, the only line with {guest_name}. The prompt now had four slots. The filler still filled five values, found no slot for guest_name and dropped it silently, 412 times. The model saw an example letter that began "Dear Hortense" and no other name, so it wrote the likeliest letter: one to Hortense. The 16:00 proof card had already been read on version 7, and the run started by itself at 01:00. This case is "we changed the prompt with no version or rollout"; a6e06 was a step nobody could see, and a6e09 is a model that changed. What can go wrong: a template tool that ignores spare values turns a missing slot into silence, so check what yours does.

steps.title: Prompts as code: numbered versions in the same history.
steps.text: Treat the prompt as part of the product's code. Keep it as a file in the repository, the shared place where the code and its full history of changes are kept, and give every change a version number. The settings the model runs with, such as which model and how long a card may be, live beside it: together they are the feature's configuration, its settings kept as files rather than typed into a live page. Now the template filler and the prompt change in the same history, and a reviewer sees both. Langfuse, a prompt management tool, says versions provide an immutable history of every prompt change, and that each update creates a new version (1, 2, 3...). What can go wrong: a history only helps if the running shop reads the version the history says is live.

steps.title: Checks on every save, then 5 cards first.
steps.text: On every save, in order. First the slot check compares the prompt's slots with the values the code fills, and fails the change if either side has one the other lacks: version 8 fails on guest_name, the retyped copy on rsvp_by. Second the ten-card eval runs ten made-up guests through the new version: each card must begin with that guest's name and carry the reply-by date. Version 8 scores 0 of 10. Third, a version that passes goes live only for a proof batch: behind a flag, the run's first 5 cards use it and the rest wait for a person to approve. With only that on, version 8 stops at 01:02:30 with 5 cards wasted. Last, rollback: one switch puts version 7 back. This is the pipeline of s5e09, The Assembly Line, with the prompt as one more file the checks run on. The proof batch is the canary release of Dead Letter s6e08, Canary in the Mine, applied to a prompt. What can go wrong: an eval only catches what it tests; the proof batch is there for what it doesn't.

steps.title: Why the quick fixes miss.
steps.text: Locking the page to Mr Tibbald changes who edits, not how: replayed with the same slip, 412 "Dear Hortense" cards by 04:26. Reading every card in the morning takes 412 x 20 seconds, 2 hours 17 minutes 20 seconds, finishing at 09:17:20, and the cards are already printed. Retyping from memory brings the names back and loses the reply-by date, because there was no version to return to. Build Night G7 builds the general mechanism: hot config reload, changing a running service's settings without dropping connections. A prompt version is the same idea: change what is live by switching a pointer, and switch it back the same way.

diagram.aria: The fix. Sibylla's 23:10 edit is saved as version 8. The slot check compares its 4 slots with the 5 values the code fills and fails it on guest_name. A version that passes goes on to the ten-card eval, where version 8 scores 0 of 10, then to a proof batch of the first 5 cards behind a flag, and only when approved to the full run of 412 cards. Version 7 stays live, and rolling back to it is one step.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. A save becomes a numbered version and meets the slot check first; version 8 fails there, on guest_name. A version that passes meets the ten-card eval, then prints only the first 5 cards behind a flag, and goes to the full run of 412 only when a person approves. Until then version 7 stays live, and switching back to it is one step.

fix.title: The fix: prompts as numbered versions, checked against the code, rolled out on 5 cards first
fix.text: Move the prompt and its settings out of the admin page into numbered files in the same history as the template filler's code. On every save, run a slot check that fails the change if the code fills a value the prompt has no slot for, or the prompt has a slot the code never fills; then a ten-card eval of made-up guests whose cards must begin with their own names and carry the reply-by date. A version that passes prints only the night's first 5 cards behind a flag, and the rest of the run waits for a person to approve. Keep the last good version live until then, and make rollback one switch back to its number.

limits: The slot check catches a missing or extra slot, not a bad letter. A version with every slot that reads coldly, or misspells the venue, passes it; only the eval and the 5 proof cards can catch that.
A proof batch needs a person to look at 5 cards at 01:00. If nobody is there, the run waits, and a late edit can delay the whole night.
Versions protect only what is kept in them. Settings left on the admin page can still change cards with no number and no check.

explain.seniorTake: A prompt is code that happens to be written in English: changing it changes what the product does, so it deserves the same care. Keep prompts and model settings as configuration in version control, beside the code that fills them, with numbered versions and a named author for each change. Check the fit mechanically: every variable the code passes must have a slot, and every slot a value, and fail the build otherwise, since many template tools fail silently. Run a small eval on every change. Roll a new prompt out gradually behind a flag or a label, watch the first outputs, and keep rollback as a pointer move to the last good version, never a rewrite from memory. Access control is still worth having, but it decides who can change a prompt, not whether a change is safe.

realWorld.title: Langfuse: versions are an immutable history
realWorld.text: Langfuse's prompt data model page says versions provide an immutable history of every prompt change, and that each update creates a new version (1, 2, 3...). It also says you can add variables to your prompts that can be dynamically filled out at runtime, which are this case's slots.

realWorld.title: Labels point at versions; code points at labels
realWorld.text: The same page says labels are pointers to specific versions, and your code would typically point to labels. The running app asks for a label, not a text, so changing what is live means moving the label.

realWorld.title: Rollback by moving the production label
realWorld.text: Langfuse's version control page says each prompt version is automatically assigned a version ID, that the latest label points to the most recently created version, and that when using a prompt without specifying a label, Langfuse will serve the version with the production label. It says you can quickly rollback to a previous version by setting the production label to that previous version, and that labels can be used to assign prompts to environments (staging, production).

realWorld.title: A deliberate production choice
realWorld.text: Langfuse's get-started page recommends using the production label to fetch the version intentionally chosen for production.

asked: How would you manage prompts in production?
How do you roll out a prompt change safely?
How do you roll back a bad prompt?
interview.answer: I treat prompts as code. Each prompt lives in version control or a prompt management tool as numbered, immutable versions, alongside the model settings it needs and the code that fills its variables, so every change has an author, a date and a review. On every change, automated checks run: the variables the code passes must match the template's placeholders exactly, because many template engines ignore extras or fill blanks silently, and a small regression eval must pass. Then I roll the new version out gradually: behind a flag or a label, to a small share of traffic or a small first batch, and I look at those outputs before widening. The app asks for a label like production rather than a text, so rollback is moving that label back to the previous version: one step, seconds, no rewriting. And I record the prompt version on every request, so when outputs change I can see which version did it.

terms.def: The person who runs a print shop's printers overnight: loads card, starts and watches the run, counts and stacks. Yannick at Larkwhistle Press.
One test card printed and read by a person before the real run. Larkwhistle prints one every afternoon at 16:00.

The written instructions sent to the model with every request. Larkwhistle's says what to write, gives an example letter, and ends with the guest's details.
A sample card inside the prompt, for the model to copy the style of. Larkwhistle's begins "Dear Hortense"; with no other name given, the model copied it.
A private web page for running a business's system. Larkwhistle's prompt lived in a text box there, and saving it changed the next run at once.
A gap in a prompt marked with curly brackets, such as {guest_name}, for a value to be put into. Also called a variable or placeholder.
Text with slots in it, like a form with blanks. Larkwhistle's prompt is a template.
The small program that puts each value from the order sheet into its slot. Larkwhistle's quietly drops a value that has no slot.
A couple's order: the couple, the date, the venue, each guest's name and the reply-by date.
The date guests must answer an invitation by, often called the RSVP date, from the French for please reply. Filled into the {rsvp_by} slot.
A saved, numbered copy of a text or program as it was at one change, so earlier ones can be compared or used again. Larkwhistle's box kept none.
Keeping every change to a set of files as a numbered or named version, with who made it and when, so any earlier one can be compared or restored.
Never changed once saved. An immutable version stays exactly as it was; a change makes a new version instead.
The live system real customers use, as opposed to a test copy such as staging (s5e09). In Langfuse, also the name of the label the app asks for.
The version the running system is using right now. Version 7 was live until 23:10.
The shared place where a project's code and the full history of its changes are kept (s5e09).

The settings a program runs with, kept as files rather than typed into a live page, so they are versioned and checked like code. For a model feature: the prompt, which model, and limits like card length.
Comparing a prompt's slots with the values the code fills, one by one: every value needs a slot, every slot a value.
An automatic check, run on every save, that fails the change when the code fills a value the prompt has no slot for, or the reverse.
A test of what a model writes: known inputs and a rule that marks each output (a5e05).
Larkwhistle's eval: ten made-up guests run through a new version. Each card must begin with that guest's name and carry the reply-by date. Version 8 scores 0 of 10.
The first 5 cards of a run, printed with a new version; the rest wait until a person approves them. Version 8 stops there at 01:02:30.
A switch, read while the system runs, that turns something on or off without changing code, like a light switch. Here it decides which cards use a new version.
How a change reaches users: all at once, or a little first and then the rest.
Sending a change to a small share first, like a miner's canary, and widening it only if all is well (a5e05). Dead Letter s6e08 covers it for code.
Going back to the last good version. With numbered versions, one switch; with none, a rewrite from memory.
The chain of automatic steps from a saved change to the running system, where a failed step stops the change (s5e09).
A tool for managing prompts and tracing model features. It keeps numbered prompt versions and labels that point at them.
In Langfuse, a name such as production that points at one prompt version. The app asks for the label, so moving it changes what is live.
The course's hands-on build of hot config reload: changing a running service's settings without dropping connections.
Changing a running service's settings while it keeps serving, without restarting it. A prompt version switch is the same idea for prompts.
An agreed way of making changes: recorded, tested and approved before they go live, with a way back.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A control 8.32 covers change management.
An audit report on a company's controls, against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. Criterion CC8.1 covers how changes are authorised, tested and approved.

atWork: Look for a production prompt that lives in an admin page or a database field and is edited live: saving it changes the next request, there is no history of earlier texts, and the only way back is someone's memory. It is a common pattern, especially where the people who write prompts aren't the people who write code. Ask four things. Where is the prompt that served yesterday's requests, word for word? What checks that the variables your code passes match the template's slots, and does your template tool fail or stay silent when they don't? What runs on a prompt change before it reaches every user: an eval, a small first share, a person's look? And how long does rollback take, and is it a pointer move or a rewrite? Build Night G7, hot config reload, builds the general mechanism; a labelled prompt version is the same idea. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 8.32 (change management) expects changes to information processing facilities and systems to follow change management procedures; and if you report under SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 covers authorising, testing and approving changes before they go live. A production prompt is such a change, so a numbered version with its eval results and approver is the evidence those controls look for. Building it in from the first prompt is far cheaper than reconstructing a history before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's support assistant writes refund emails from a prompt kept in a text field of its admin tool. After a colleague tidied the prompt on Friday evening, every refund email says "your order #10442", the order number in the prompt's example email. Nothing errored. What probably happened, and what would you put in place?

keyIdeas.idea: The tidy-up removed the order number's slot; the filler dropped the value without an error, and the model copied the example's number
Keep prompts as numbered versions in the same history as the code, so a bad one can be rolled back
Check before it goes live: slots against the values the code fills, a small eval, a small first batch

recall.model: The tidy-up probably deleted the line holding the order number's placeholder. The code still passed the number, the template tool silently dropped a value with no slot, and the model, given no number, copied the one in the example email. Nothing errored because nothing checked the fit. I'd keep the prompt as numbered versions in version control, in the same history as the code that fills it, so Friday's version can be rolled back in one step. Then I'd check every change against the code: each value the code fills needs a slot and each slot a value, or the build fails. A small eval of test cases runs on every change, and a new version goes to a small first batch of emails before the rest.

recall.prompt: Larkwhistle prints 2 cards a minute from 01:00. With a proof batch of the first 5 cards on, and version 8 saved at 23:10, when does the run stop, and how many cards are wasted?
options: Never: the proof batch only reads cards
recall.why: Each card takes 30 seconds, so the 5th is done at 01:00 + 2 minutes 30 seconds = 01:02:30. All 5 begin "Dear Hortense", the run waits for a person, and rolling back to version 7 prints the 412 right cards by 04:28:30. Only those 5 are wasted.

recall.prompt: A teammate says prompts are just text and don't need the same care as the app's source files. What would you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Changing a prompt changes what the product does, just as changing code does
Without numbered versions there is nothing to roll back to
Test a change before everyone gets it: an eval, then a small first batch

recall.model: A prompt change changes what the product does just as much as a code change, and often more quietly. Keep prompts as numbered versions beside the code, so the last good one is always there: without that, rollback means rewriting from memory, which is how a missing line comes back. And test each change before everyone gets it: an eval on every save, then a small batch first, the first few outputs read before the rest go out.

recall.prompt: Sibylla's retyped prompt has slots for couple, date, venue and guest_name. The code fills those four and rsvp_by. What does the slot check report?
options: Nothing: every slot has a value
It fails: the code fills rsvp_by, and the prompt has no slot for it
It fails: guest_name has no value
It passes, and the eval fails on names
recall.why: The check compares both ways. Every slot has a value, but the code fills rsvp_by and there is nowhere to put it, so the template filler would drop it and every card would lose its reply-by date. The ten-card eval would also fail, 0 of 10, on the missing date, not on names.

recall.prompt: In Langfuse, how do you roll back to the previous prompt version?
options: Edit the newest version back by hand
Set the production label on the previous version
Create a new prompt with a new name
recall.why: Langfuse's version control page says you can quickly rollback to a previous version by setting the production label to that previous version. Versions are an immutable history, and the code asks for the label, so moving it changes what is live.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. Every prompt change is now a numbered version with the slot check, the ten-card eval and 5 proof cards, and nothing has gone wrong. But the model's other settings, such as the longest a card may be, are still boxes on the admin page. On Tuesday Mr Tibbald cut that length from 90 words to 40 for a christening order's small cards and didn't put it back. Wednesday's 01:00 run printed 188 wedding cards, each stopping mid-sentence before the reply-by date. The prompt hadn't changed, so no check ran.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did nothing catch it, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The length is part of what makes a card, but it sat outside the versions and the checks
Keep the settings in the same numbered version as the prompt
Run the checks on any change to either, and give the other product its own settings

coldCase.model: The prompt was protected and the length wasn't. A card's length is part of the configuration as much as the prompt is, but it was not versioned: a live box on the admin page, outside the checks. Keep the model settings in the same file as the prompt, together with it in one version, so any change to either makes a new number and runs the slot check, the eval and the proof cards. The eval would have failed at once: no card carried the reply-by date. And give the christening cards their own settings, a separate entry per product, so changing one can't reach the other.

sources.title: Langfuse documentation, Prompt management, Data model, read 15 October 2026: Versions provide an immutable history of every prompt change; Each update creates a new version (1, 2, 3...); Labels are pointers to specific versions; Your code would typically point to labels; You can add variables to your prompts that can be dynamically filled out at runtime

Langfuse documentation, Prompt management, Version control, read 15 October 2026: Each prompt version is automatically assigned a version ID; Labels can be used to assign prompts to environments (staging, production); The latest label points to the most recently created version; Langfuse will serve the version with the production label; You can quickly rollback to a previous version by setting the production label to that previous version

Langfuse documentation, Prompt management, Get started, read 15 October 2026: We recommend using the production label to fetch the version intentionally chosen for production; By default, the prompt labeled production is returned
